questions.question: How do @SpringBootTest test slices work and how does Spring Boot cache test application contexts?
questions.title: Spring Boot Testing: @SpringBootTest, Slices, and Context Caching
questions.direct_answer: `@SpringBootTest` loads the **full application context** and is suitable for integration tests, but it is slow. **Test slice annotations** like `@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, and `@JsonTest` load only the slice of the context relevant to the test (controllers, JPA layer, JSON serialization), making them much faster. Spring Test **caches `ApplicationContext`s** across test classes that share identical configuration — so the expensive context startup happens once per unique configuration combination. The cache key includes `@MockBean` declarations, `@ActiveProfiles`, and `@TestPropertySource` — variation in any of those creates a separate context.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `@SpringBootTest` for every test including repository-only or controller-only tests, causing very slow test suites, or accidentally breaking context caching by adding test-specific `@MockBean` in a way that creates a unique context per test class
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that `@MockBean` creates a new `ApplicationContext` (breaking caching) so it should be standardized in a base class or `@TestConfiguration`, and mention the cache logging at `org.springframework.test.context.cache=DEBUG`

sections.title: Why @SpringBootTest Makes Your Test Suite Slow — and Slices Exist to Fix It
sections.content:
The most common Spring Boot testing mistake is using `@SpringBootTest` for everything.
- Every `@SpringBootTest` loads the full application context — database connections, message brokers, all auto-configurations, every bean.
- For a test that only checks a controller's request mapping or a repository's query, **you're paying 10-30 seconds of context startup for a test that runs in milliseconds**.

**Test slices solve this** by loading only the beans relevant to one layer. `@WebMvcTest` loads controllers, filters, and MVC infrastructure — no services, no repositories, no database. `@DataJpaTest` loads JPA repositories with an embedded database — no controllers, no web server. Each slice auto-configures just enough context for its layer.

But slices introduce a second problem: **context caching**.
- Spring's test framework caches application contexts across tests to avoid re-creating them.
- The cache key is the combination of configuration classes, properties, active profiles, and **mock definitions**.
- Any difference creates a new context.
- Understanding what breaks the cache is the difference between a test suite that runs in 2 minutes and one that takes 15.

sections.title: Test Slice Annotations — What Each Loads
sections.content:
Each slice annotation is a meta-annotation that combines `@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)` with `@AutoConfigure*` annotations specific to one layer.

| Annotation | Loads | Doesn't Load | Use For |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@SpringBootTest` | Full context | — | End-to-end integration tests |
| `@WebMvcTest` | MVC controllers, filters, advice | Services, repositories, DB | Controller routing and validation |
| `@WebFluxTest` | Reactive controllers, WebFilter | Services, R2DBC | Reactive controller tests |
| `@DataJpaTest` | JPA repos + embedded H2, transactional | Web layer, services | Repository queries, mappings |
| `@DataMongoTest` | MongoDB repos | Web, JPA | Mongo repository tests |
| `@JsonTest` | Jackson, Gson configuration | Everything else | Serialization unit tests |
| `@RestClientTest` | `RestTemplate`/`RestClient` config | Everything else | HTTP client tests with `MockRestServiceServer` |

**Pick the smallest slice that exercises the behavior**. A controller test should not start a database; a repository test should not start MVC.

sections.title: Test Slice Examples
Context Caching — What Shares and What Breaks the Cache
Slice and Caching Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When slices help:**
- Fast feedback on focused concerns — one controller, one repository, one serializer
- Clear separation between unit and integration tests in CI
- Maximum context cache reuse when slices share base configuration

**When slices hurt:**
- Cross-cutting tests that span layers — slice mocks the wrong dependency
- H2-based `@DataJpaTest` masks dialect-specific bugs that fail in PostgreSQL
- Slice annotations sometimes forget to import `@TestConfiguration` classes you actually need

**Watch for:**
- `@MockBean` declared per-test — kills caching; standardize in a base class
- `@TestPropertySource` with one-off values — same caching problem
- `@DirtiesContext` used to mask test isolation issues — fix the root cause instead
- Mixing `@SpringBootTest` with slices in the same suite — they don't share contexts
- H2 dialect differences from PostgreSQL — switch to Testcontainers for production fidelity

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootTest` loads the full application context — use it only for integration tests** — `@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, `@JsonTest` load sliced contexts with only the relevant beans.
- **`@MockBean` breaks context caching** — each unique `@MockBean` configuration creates a separate `ApplicationContext`; standardize mocks in a base test class.
- **`@DataJpaTest` uses an embedded H2 by default** — add `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` to test against the real database; pair with Testcontainers in CI.
- **`@WebMvcTest` tests the web layer only** — no `@Service` or `@Repository` beans; use `@MockBean` to replace them; tests are fast because no database or message broker is started.
- **Context caching key includes `@ActiveProfiles`, `@TestPropertySource`, and `@MockBean`** — minimize variation to maximize cache hits.
- **Enable `org.springframework.test.context.cache=DEBUG`** — logs cache hits and misses; surfaces accidental cache busts immediately.
- **`@DirtiesContext` evicts a context** — use only when state mutation is unavoidable; otherwise solve the underlying isolation issue.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot provides test slice annotations that load only the beans relevant to what you are testing. Using `@SpringBootTest` for everything works but is unnecessarily slow — a repository test that starts the web layer and message brokers wastes seconds on every CI run.

**Test slices**
- `@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)` — loads only MVC infrastructure, the specified controller, and related `@ControllerAdvice`; no database, no service layer; use `@MockBean` for dependencies
- `@DataJpaTest` — loads only JPA/Hibernate + an embedded H2 database; no web layer; tests repository logic in isolation
- `@SpringBootTest` — loads the full `ApplicationContext`; use for end-to-end integration tests only

**Context caching**
- Spring caches `ApplicationContext` instances across test classes that share the same configuration
- `@MockBean` is the most common cache-buster — each unique set of mocked beans creates a distinct context
- Extract shared mocks into a base test class or `@TestConfiguration` class to maximize cache hits across the test suite
- Enable `org.springframework.test.context.cache=DEBUG` to see cache hits and misses

**Embedded vs real database**
- `@DataJpaTest` defaults to H2; if your query uses a PostgreSQL-specific function, the test passes with H2 and fails in production
- `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` + Testcontainers runs the real database in CI — the only reliable approach for dialect-specific queries

In an interview, the strong answer is: **slices for fast focused tests, full `@SpringBootTest` for end-to-end paths, and a base class to keep mock signatures consistent so the cache actually works**.

questions.question: How do you integrate Testcontainers with @SpringBootTest for production-fidelity integration tests?
questions.title: Testcontainers with @SpringBootTest — The Integration Pattern
questions.direct_answer: Use Testcontainers to run the **real database, message broker, or cache** in a Docker container during integration tests, eliminating H2-vs-PostgreSQL dialect drift. The modern pattern in Spring Boot 3.1+ uses **`@ServiceConnection`** which auto-wires container connection details into Spring properties — no manual `@DynamicPropertySource` plumbing. Make containers `static final` with `withReuse(true)` and a shared `@TestConfiguration` so the same container is reused across the entire test suite, preserving Spring's context cache. The combination gives you production-fidelity tests at a few seconds of startup overhead per CI run, not per test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can set up integration tests that run against the real database/broker without breaking Spring's context cache or tanking CI runtime
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a new container per test class with `@Container` instance fields, forcing Docker startup on every test class and breaking context caching
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention `@ServiceConnection` (Spring Boot 3.1+), container reuse with `~/.testcontainers.properties`, and `Testcontainers.exposeHostPorts` for callbacks back to the host

sections.title: H2 Lies — Testcontainers Tells the Truth
sections.content:
**The H2 problem is real**. `@DataJpaTest` defaults to an embedded H2 database, which silently passes tests for queries that fail against PostgreSQL or MySQL in production.
- JSONB operators, window functions, full-text search, custom types, even basic things like `RETURNING` clauses behave differently.
- A test suite that's green against H2 is no guarantee of correctness against the real database.

**Testcontainers solves this** by running the actual database (or Kafka, Redis, RabbitMQ, Elasticsearch, S3 via LocalStack) in a Docker container during the test run.
- Your code talks to the same engine in tests as in production.
- The only cost is a few seconds of container startup at CI initialization.

**Spring Boot 3.1+ added `@ServiceConnection`** which makes the integration nearly invisible.
- Annotate a `static` container field with `@ServiceConnection` and Spring Boot auto-configures the JDBC URL, Kafka bootstrap servers, or Redis connection from the running container — no `@DynamicPropertySource`, no manual property wiring.
- Combined with **container reuse** (`withReuse(true)`), the same container survives across multiple `mvn test` runs locally, making the developer feedback loop nearly as fast as H2 with full PostgreSQL fidelity.

sections.title: Setup — Dependencies and Reuse Configuration
sections.content:
**Maven dependencies**

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>testcontainers</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-testcontainers</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

**Enable container reuse on the developer machine**
- Create `~/.testcontainers.properties` once per developer
- Contents: `testcontainers.reuse.enable=true`
- Containers persist across `mvn test` runs locally; CI typically disables reuse for hermetic builds

**Spring Boot version requirement**
- Spring Boot 3.1+ for `@ServiceConnection`
- Earlier versions: use `@DynamicPropertySource` to wire container URLs into Spring properties manually

sections.title: The Modern Pattern with @ServiceConnection
The Pre-3.1 Pattern with @DynamicPropertySource
Testcontainers Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When Testcontainers helps:**
- Repository and integration tests where DB dialect differences matter (JSONB, window functions, custom types)
- Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis tests that need real protocol semantics
- LocalStack containers for AWS S3, SQS, DynamoDB integration
- Schema migration tests that must run real Flyway against the real engine

**When Testcontainers hurts:**
- Pure unit tests that exercise no I/O — overkill
- CI environments without Docker support
- Constrained hosts where Docker daemon overhead is significant
- Test classes that create one container per class — Docker startup time tanks the suite

**Watch for:**
- Forgetting `withReuse(true)` — containers restart per JVM and slow local development
- Reuse enabled in CI — CI should be hermetic; reuse on developer machines only
- Mixing `@DataJpaTest` with Testcontainers — `@DataJpaTest` replaces the DataSource; add `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)`
- Container image versions drifting from production — pin exact tags, not `latest`
- Network mode issues on macOS / Windows where Docker runs in a VM and host networking differs

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ServiceConnection` in Spring Boot 3.1+** — auto-configures Spring properties from a container bean; no `@DynamicPropertySource` needed.
- **`static final` containers with `withReuse(true)`** — one container per JVM, persistent across local runs when `~/.testcontainers.properties` enables reuse.
- **Shared `@TestConfiguration`** — import the same container config into every `@SpringBootTest`; same context cache, same container, fast suite.
- **`@DataJpaTest` + `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)`** — runs `@DataJpaTest` against the real Testcontainers DataSource instead of H2.
- **Pin exact image tags** — `postgres:16-alpine`, not `postgres:latest`; reproducibility across machines.
- **CI typically disables reuse** — hermetic builds; reuse is a developer-machine optimization.
- **Testcontainers supports almost everything** — PostgreSQL, MySQL, Kafka, Redis, RabbitMQ, Elasticsearch, MongoDB, LocalStack (AWS), Selenium browsers.
- **`Testcontainers.exposeHostPorts(...)`** — for callbacks where the container needs to reach a port on the host.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Testcontainers runs the real database, message broker, or cache in a Docker container during integration tests so your code talks to the same engine in tests as in production. The H2 default in `@DataJpaTest` is fine for trivial CRUD but silently passes tests for PostgreSQL-specific features that fail in production.

**The modern Spring Boot 3.1+ pattern**
- Annotate a `static` container bean with `@ServiceConnection` in a `@TestConfiguration` class
- Spring Boot auto-configures `spring.datasource.url`, Kafka bootstrap servers, Redis host/port from the running container
- Import the configuration into every `@SpringBootTest` — the same context cache and the same container are reused across the suite

**The pre-3.1 pattern**
- `@Container static PostgreSQLContainer postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer(...)` plus `@DynamicPropertySource` to wire the URL into Spring properties
- Verbose but works for older Spring Boot versions

**The two patterns that make it fast**
- `static final` container fields — one container per JVM, not per test class
- `withReuse(true)` plus `~/.testcontainers.properties` enabling reuse — container persists across `mvn test` runs locally

**Common pitfalls**
- Non-static `@Container` fields start a new container per test class — kills the context cache and slows the suite
- Forgetting `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` when using `@DataJpaTest` with Testcontainers — Spring replaces the DataSource with H2
- Pinning to `:latest` image tags — reproducibility issues across machines

In an interview, the strong answer is: **`@ServiceConnection` + `static final` containers + `withReuse(true)` + a shared `@TestConfiguration` is the production-fidelity integration test pattern that doesn't break Spring's context cache or balloon CI time**.
